planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in January-February while dormant; Flordaguard requires only about 150 chill hours, a University of Florida release grown both as a very-low-chill fruiting peach and widely used as a root-knot nematode-resistant rootstock.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Flordaguard is a University of Florida release with an exceptionally low chill requirement of roughly 150 hours, making it one of the few peaches that reliably flowers and fruits in the mildest winters of the Gulf South and peninsular Florida, and it is separately valued in the nursery trade as a root-knot nematode-resistant rootstock for grafting less-hardy peach cultivars. Its own fruit is small to medium, clingstone, and mainly ornamental to fair-eating quality, with showy pink spring flowers that make it attractive even where fruit quality is secondary. Thin fruit if a heavier crop sets than the tree can properly size, and prune to an open-center vase shape after leaf drop.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Peach Variety Selection for Texas and the Gulf Coast

common_name: Republic of Texas Fig (Cold-Hardy Brown Sugar Fig)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or rooted cuttings after last frost; Republic of Texas is an exceptionally cold-hardy, drought-tolerant Texas heirloom fig that reliably resprouts from the roots even after a hard freeze kills the top growth.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Republic of Texas is among the most cold-hardy and drought-tolerant fig cultivars grown in Texas home orchards, tolerating both harder winter freezes and drier soil than many other figs. Fruit is medium-sized with brownish-purple skin and sweet, deep amber-pink flesh with a rich, honeyed flavor, ripening over a long harvest window from summer into fall. Even where winter cold kills the top growth to the ground, the vigorous root system reliably resprouts and fruits again the following year, making it a forgiving choice for the cooler edge of fig-growing range. Prune to control size and remove winter-killed wood in spring once new growth reveals what survived.
sources: LSU AgCenter — Fig Varieties for Louisiana Gardeners

common_name: O'Henry Sweet Potato (White-Skin White-Flesh Beauregard Sport)

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F; O'Henry is a white-skinned, white-fleshed sport of Beauregard with a milder, less sweet flavor than orange-fleshed types.

directions: O'Henry arose as a natural sport of Beauregard, sharing its parent's vigor and productivity but with cream-white skin and white flesh in place of Beauregard's copper skin and orange flesh, giving a milder, less sweet, drier-textured potato favored by cooks who want a sweet potato that behaves more like a baking potato. Vines are vigorous and trailing, producing heavy yields of smooth, uniform, blocky roots under the same growing conditions Beauregard thrives in. Cure freshly dug roots at warm temperature and high humidity for about a week before storage to heal skin cuts and convert starches to sugars, improving both flavor and keeping quality. Roots can develop pronounced lenticels if soil stays wet close to harvest, so time digging for a dry stretch.
sources: Louisiana State University sweet potato variety trials
